paragraphs.text: A loose [green tea](green:definition) grown on [Taiwan](taiwan:on-a-label) in 1950. The label names only the island, not a mountain or township, so the place stops there. Taiwan's tea came from Fujian, and its trade is built on [oolong](taiwan:known-for), but green tea is made there too.
The leaf was never allowed to oxidise. Soon after picking it was [fixed](green:making) with heat to stop its own enzymes before they could turn it brown, then rolled and dried so it would keep.

Seventy-six years is far past the year or two that green tea is usually kept. The sources describe no tradition of [ageing green tea](green:ageing), and the type promises nothing over time, so how this tea was kept counts for more than its years.

brewing.text: Green tea takes water well below the boil, about 80°C, a little cooler for the youngest leaf and a little warmer for older, larger leaf. Boiling water draws out bitterness and dries the cup. A common start is about 2 grams of leaf to 100 ml, in a glass or a small gaiwan, with short steeps of half a minute to two minutes, and the same leaf can be brewed a few times.

notice.text: A fresh, clean cup that many call crisp, with a sweet, soft finish, and a pale green to yellow-green liquor. The smell runs from fresh leaf to flowers, and steamed teas lean grassy or seaweed-like. Too much heat or too long a steep turns the cup bitter and drying.
